la:adj:lassus.html:
lassus, a, um, adj.
etym. dub.; acc. to Bopp, Gloss. 112, 6, for glassus from glasnus; kindred to Sanscr. glasnu, fessus, defessus, lassus; but more prob. collat. form of laxus; cf. langueo
,
faint, languid, weary, tired, exhausted (syn.: fessus, fatigatus, defatigatus; mostly poet. and in post-Aug. prose; not in Cic. or Cæs.).
Lit.: lassus de via,: opere faciundo,: lassus jam sum durando miser,; cf.: Romani itinere atque opere castrorum et proelio fessi lassique erant,: recto itinere lassi,: assiduo gaudio, : ab equo indomito,: lasso mihi subvenire,: alieno aratro,: marris ac vomere,.—Prov.: a lasso rixam quaeri (because tired persons are easily vexed),.—
With gen.: lassus maris et viarum Militiaeque,; cf.: ita me amor lassum animi ludificat,.—
With acc.: lassus pondus,. —
With inf.: nec fueris nomen lassa vocare meum, (3, 5, 12); 2, 15 (3, 7), 46; 2, 33 (3, 31), 26.—
Transf., of things: fructious assiduis lassa humus,exhausted,; cf.: lassa et effeta natura,: aurae spatio ipso,: stomachus,: verba onerantia lassas aures,: collum,drooping,: lasso collo jumenta,: undae,i. e. become calm again,: mons,gently sloping,: si res lassa labat, Itidem amici collabascunt,.—Comp., sup., and adv. seem not to occur.

la:verb:lasso.gloss: to exhaust; to fatigue; to tire; to weary; to wear out or wear down; to render faint
senses: to exhaust; to fatigue; to tire; to weary; to wear out or wear down; to render faint
la:verb:lasso.html:
lasso, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
lassus
,
to render faint or languid, to tire, weary, fatigue, to deprive of vigor (syn.: fatigo, languefacio; perh. not ante-Aug.): aliquem,: laevam,: longior infirmum ne lasset epistola corpus,: brachia plagis, cf.: lassata gravi ceciderunt brachia massā,: visu lassatur inani,: oculos,: jam vitia primo fervore adulescentiae indomita lassavit,; ; ; ; ; : numina,to weary with petitions,: Cecropiam Cotytto,.—Transf.: sidus Hyperborei Bootae,i. e. to bear steadfastly,: lassatum fluctibus aequor,i. e. become calm,: ventus lassatur,: lassata triumphis fortuna,.—In mal. part., ; .

la:adj:lascivus.html:
lascīvus, a, um, adj.
Sanscr. lash-āmi, desire; las-āmi, play; Gr. la- in λάω, λιλαίομαι; cf. Goth. lustus; also Lat. largus
,
wanton, petulant, sportive, playful, frolicsome, frisky, (syn.: petulans, procax).
In a good sense: nova proles, * : capella,: puella,: pueri,: Amores,: currumque sequuntur matris lascivo sidera fulva choro,: tenero lascivior haedo,: aetas,: hederae,wanton, luxuriant,: acus,for ornamenting the hair, a hair-pin,; cf. : tristia maestum Vultum verba decent. ... Ludentem lasciva,sportive, playful,; cf.: quod dicitur, aut est lascivum et hilare aut contumeliosum,: ad quod (caput aselli) lascivi ludebant ruris alumni,. —
In a bad sense, licentious, lewd, lustful, lascivious, : Siculi, ut sunt lascivi et dicaces, Cael. ap. : puellae,lascivious,: femur,: libelli,lewd,; cf.: tabellis ac sigillis lascivissimarum picturarum et figurarum,.—
Trop., of style, licentious, luxuriant, overloaded with ornament; oratio, ; cf.: illud lascivum ζωὴ καὶ ψυχή, .—Hence, adv. in two forms.
lascīvē, wantonly, lasciviously (post-class.): loqui,licentiously,: versus facere,. —Comp.: lascivius,.—
lascīvĭter, wantonly, petulantly: ludere, Laev. ap. P.

la:verb:lascivio.gloss: to frolic; to be lively or merry
senses: to frolic; to be lively or merry
la:verb:lascivio.html:
lascīvĭo, ĭi, ītum, 4, v. n.
lascivus
,
to be wanton, petulant, sportive, to sport, frisk, frolic (not freq. till after the Aug. per.).
Lit.: licet lascivire, dum nihil metuas, *: Ap. Claudius ait, lascivire magis plebem quam saevire,: licentiam lasciviendi permittere militi,: eo principio lascivire miles,: exsilit agnus Lascivitque fuga,and wantonly frisks away,; cf. : angues ... lascivientium piscium modo exsultasse,. —Poet.: dextera lascivit caesa Tegeatide capra (of the Luperci, who wantonly struck at passers-by),: ferratus lascivit apex,: quis lascivit aquis et ab aethere ludit,. —Esp.: in Venerem,to be lascivious,.—
Trop., to indulge in license of language or style (a favorite expression of Quintilian): lascivimus syntonorum modis saltitantes,; cf. : toto et rerum et verborum et compositionis genere lasciviunt,: puerilibus sententiolis,; cf. ; : Ovidius lascivire in Metamorphosesi solet,.

la:noun:lascivia.html:
lascīvĭa, ae, f.
lascivus
,
sportiveness, playfulness, frolicsomeness, jollity.
In a good sense (class.): adulescens plenus amoris ac lasciviae,: hilaritas et lascivia,: laeta (agrestium),: ut nudi juvenes, Lycaeum Pana venerantes, per lusum atque lasciviam currerent, Drak.: in juvenales lusus lasciviamque versi,; : piscium, Pac. ap. : si quid per lasciviam, et non data opera ut furtum committeretur, factum sit,.—Of inanim. things: naturae,.—Comic.: o virgarum lascivia,thou scourge's pastime!.—
In a bad sense, wantonness, licentiousness, petulance, impudence, lewdness, lasciviousness (mostly postAug.; not in Cic.): quos soluto imperio licentia corruperat,; with superbia,: maledicendi,: theatralis populi,: lasciviae

notae, of lewdness, ; cf.: Caesonia luxuriae ac lasciviae perditae,: ignoscitur, nisi in lata et incauta neglegentia vel lascivia fuit, Mos. et Rom. Leg. Coll. 12, 5, 2; cf. l. l. supra. —Of a licentious, prolix style: lasciviae flosculis capi,: alios recens haec lascivia deliciaeque et omnia ad voluptatem multitudinis imperitae composita delectant,: lasciviam a vobis prohibetote,impious exultation, Gronov. ad loc.

la:noun:lassitudo.html:
lassĭtūdo, ĭnis, f.
id.
,
faintness, weariness, heaviness, lassitude (class.): exercitationis finis esse debet lassitudo, quae citra fatigationem est,: omnia membra lassitudo mihi tenet,: lassitudinem hercle verba tua mihi addunt,: lassitudinem alicui eximere,: sedare,: illic (in lapicidinis) ibi demumst locus, ubi labore lassitudost exigunda ex corpore,: artius ex lassitudine dormire,: nulla lassitudo impedire officium et fidem debet,: nostros vires lassitudine deficiebant,: lassitudine confici, and 95: cursu ac lassitudine exanimati,: lassitudine oppressi,: timere, ne non virtute hostium, sed lassitudine sua vincerentur,: in lassitudine homines proniores sunt ad iracundiam,: citra lassitudinem exercere aliquid,not to weary,.—
With gen. subj.: lassitudo armorum equitandive,.—Transf., as a term of reproach: lassitudo conservūm, reduviae flagri, that wearies his fellowslaves with stripes, Titin. ap. Müll.
